blocks.title: 1. The Core Concept: Arrays of Numbers with Superpowers
blocks.content: A **Matrix** is a rectangular grid of numbers arranged in rows and columns. They might look simple, but matrices can solve systems of equations, transform 3D graphics in video games, encrypt data, and even power Google's search algorithm. A 2x2 matrix has 2 rows and 2 columns. A 3x1 matrix has 3 rows and 1 column.

blocks.title: 2. The Rules: Matrix Operations
blocks.content:
• **Addition:** Add corresponding elements (matrices must be same size).
• **Scalar multiplication:** Multiply every element by the scalar.
• **Matrix multiplication:** Row-by-column dot products. The number of columns in the first MUST equal the number of rows in the second.
• **Determinant (2x2):** For [[a,b],[c,d]], det = ad - bc.
• Matrix multiplication is NOT commutative: A*B does not equal B*A!

blocks.title: 3. Step-by-Step: Multiplying 2x2 Matrices
blocks.content:
To multiply matrix A by matrix B:

1. Take the first ROW of A and the first COLUMN of B.
2. Multiply corresponding elements and add: this gives you position (1,1) of the answer.
3. First row of A x second column of B = position (1,2).
4. Second row of A x first column of B = position (2,1).
5. Second row of A x second column of B = position (2,2).

blocks.title: 5. Common Pitfalls
blocks.content: The absolute deadliest matrix mistake: trying to multiply matrices of incompatible sizes. You can only multiply an (m x n) matrix by an (n x p) matrix. The 'inner dimensions' (n) must match! If you try to multiply a 2x3 by a 2x3, it's impossible. Also, remember: matrix multiplication is NOT commutative. A*B usually gives a completely different result from B*A.
